Floor analytics · bottom-10 review

Luck, location, or a leak?

The general manager wants to replace the 10 slot machines that earned the least. This page tests every machine on that list against three explanations before anyone spends money: luck (results swing around the expected win), location (a quiet spot or short time on the floor), and a leak (downtime, or a machine paying out more than its settings allow). The period, zone and bank controls at the top update every view.

Why each bottom-10 machine earned less

Main reason per machine, in the order we test them
Tests run in this order: leak (hit-rate check against the published paytable, |z| > 4) → short time on floor → truly weak (below peers at the same spot) → location → bad luck → low-edge game. Details in §1.
Question 1

Which machines are truly underperforming?

Ranking by raw house win mixes up five things. For each machine we split the gap to the median machine into parts that add up exactly: the game it runs, its time on the floor, downtime, its location, the machine itself (expected win compared with the same game in the same zone), and luck (actual house win minus theo).

Bottom 10 by house win: where the gap to the median machine comes from

The manager's list, tested

Click a row to see that machine's evidence. Luck z: how many standard deviations the house win is from theo, using each game's published payout variance (|z| < 2 is normal swing). Machine index: theo compared with the same game in the same zone (1.00 = average, 90% interval shown).

The fair ranking: machines that are truly weakest

Lowest machine index with at least 60% of the period on the floor. Only machines whose whole 90% interval is below 0.90 are flagged.
Index = Σ theo ÷ Σ (available hours × zone·month·weekday rate × game factor). The interval comes from day-to-day variation in that ratio.

Question 5

What did the comp program cost, and did anything change?

Points charged per $1 of comp

Daily, from loyalty_ledger redemptions. The rate dropped overnight on May 1.

Comp cost per day (cost of goods)

Daily, with 7-day average. Uses comp_cost_usd, counted once and not added to POS cost of goods.

Before and after the May 1 change

Before = Jan 1–Apr 30 (120 days); after = May 1–Jun 30 (61 days). This is a simple before/after comparison and is confounded by season (June is the weakest month across Las Vegas). That is why §6 funds a controlled pilot rather than a reversal.
Model & validation

Forecasting daily floor coin-in

We trained on January–April, froze the forecasts, then tested on May–June. The baseline is a constant training-period daily mean. The models are the weekday mean, weekday mean × an uplift for events already announced by May 1 (so the Locals Appreciation Week, announced May 26, is not flagged), and weekday mean × a linear trend. Each forecast uses only information available on May 1, 2025.

Holdout error (May–June)

Mean absolute error in dollars per day; lower is better

How we would spend $100,000 (July 1–30, 2025)

Up to three action types. Cost = quantity × (unit cost + daily cost × days left after the lead time); fixed packages are charged in full. Benefits are 30-day expected house win (theo) after the lead time and are estimates, not promises. Move the sliders to test the assumptions.

Appendix

Claims & evidence

Each claim lists the table or query it comes from, the result, the alternative explanation we tested, and its limitation. Every number is rebuilt by python analysis/build_data.py from the files in data/. The same appendix is in CLAIMS_AND_EVIDENCE.md, and the 400-word summary is in WRITEUP.md.

Method notes

Rows used. Active machine-days only (active = true). The 1,018 days before install or after retirement are excluded, not counted as zero.

Money math. Hold = Σ house win ÷ Σ coin-in (ratio of sums). Theo = Σ bet × (1 − RTP). Luck = house win − theo. Hours come from scheduled_seconds, so the 23-hour March 8 is handled.

Luck z. The variance of house win is Σ bet² × the game's payout-multiplier variance (machine_day.sum_bet_squared × game_math.payout_multiplier_variance). z = luck ÷ √variance. With 310 machines, a few |z| > 2.5 are expected by chance alone. A Bonferroni 5% cut-off is about 3.6.

Location benchmark. A multiplicative fit: theo per available hour = zone × month × weekday rate × game factor, fitted on all machines by alternating averages. The machine index is a machine's theo divided by that benchmark. Theo is used, not house win, so luck can't leak into the index.

Gap decomposition. House win − median = game (full-period theo at the floor-average location − median) + time on floor + downtime + location + machine + luck. The parts add up exactly.

Downtime value. Down hours × the machine's location-expected theo per hour. This is an upper bound, since displaced players may play a neighbouring machine.

Hit-rate leak screen. Observed payout-positive spins ÷ paid spins, compared with game_math.hit_probability using a binomial z-test. A flag is a reason to inspect, not evidence of wrongdoing.

Players. player_period, carded play only. Concentration uses each player's six-month total. Comp cost is taken once from comp_cost_usd, which is already inside POS cost of goods.

AI-use disclosure

The analysis pipeline (analysis/build_data.py) and this dashboard were written with Claude (Anthropic) via Claude Code. It wrote the pandas code, the HTML/SVG charts and the neo-brutalist styling, and drafted the text. Every number on the page is computed from the provided data by that script, and the team should review the claims before submitting.

Reproduce

python -m pip install pandas pyarrow then python analysis/build_data.py from the repository root. The script rewrites analysis/dashboard_data.json and the embedded data block in this file. Open dashboard.html in any browser; it needs no server or internet connection.

The Gilded Ace is fictional and all casino data is synthetic (release 0.9.0-draft). Only the LVCVA figures in §2 are real public data. Unusual payouts are leads to inspect, not proof of wrongdoing.
